message.content:
CONTEXT: You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ "inflection" library (Rails-style Inflector) purely as a black box.
BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test11_executable   (run from any cwd; it needs no files)
USAGE: ./test11_executable <int num> <word>    -- requires argc > 2, then prints exactly 11 lines.
LINE MAP (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  ordinalize(num)
  3  camelize(word, true)
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  titleize(word)
  6  capitalize(word)
  7  truncate(word, 5)
  8  truncate(word, 10, "~")
  9  parameterize(word)
  10 parameterize(word, "_")
  11 isPlural(word)  -> prints 0 or 1
HOW TO PROBE ONE LINE:
  /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 1 'my_word' | sed -n '3p'
Use single quotes or printf to control argv exactly. To probe words containing spaces, quotes, newlines, backslashes, or
non-ASCII UTF-8, pass them as a SINGLE argv element (e.g. "$(printf 'a\tb')" or 'héllo'). Empty word: '' (still argc>2).

ALREADY ESTABLISHED — treat as given, do NOT spend probes re-deriving:
  * pluralize(w) = w + "s", UNLESS w exactly (case-sensitively) equals one of the uncountables
      {equipment, information, rice, money, species, series, fish, sheep, jeans, police}  -> then w unchanged.
      (The library's 17 plural regex rules are dead code: the first registered rule /$/ -> "s" always matches first.)
  * isPlural(w) == (singularize(w) != w).  isSingular(w) == !isPlural(w).
  * The library registers 23 singular regex rules (Rails standard) plus a first rule /s$/ -> "" ; first match wins,
    iterating in registration order. There are NO irregular() pairs and NO human() rules (person->persons, child->childs).
  * An acronyms table exists containing exactly: HTML, HTTP, XML, JSON, API.
  * Other literals in the binary: "..." (truncate default omission), "-" (parameterize default sep), "_", " ", "::",
    "_id", "id", "th", "st", "nd", "rd".
  * The C++ is compiled with gcc-12, uses std::regex (ECMAScript grammar) and std::string (byte-oriented, no UTF-8 awareness).

OPTIONAL EXTRA TOOL: you may disassemble to resolve ambiguity (objdump and nm are at /opt/compiler/gcc-12/bin/, on PATH).
  objdump -dC --start-address=0xADDR --stop-address=0xADDR2 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
  Symbol addresses: pluralize 0x405d12, singularize 0x405f84, camelize 0x406262, underscore 0x40636e, classify 0x40649a,
  tableize 0x40650a, humanize 0x406576, titleize 0x4066fe, ordinalize 0x40681c, dasherize 0x406992, parameterize 0x406a1a,
  isPlural 0x406bc0, isSingular 0x406c0c, upcase 0x406c2a, downcase 0x406cea, capitalize 0x406daa, decapitalize 0x406ed0,
  truncate 0x406f98, demodulize 0x40705a, deconstantize 0x4070c8, foreign_key 0x40716e, ordinal 0x4071e8, initialize 0x403cd4.
  Disassembly is a tiebreaker; observed behavior is the ground truth.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT:
  * Do NOT write, create, or modify any file anywhere. Read-only + running the binary only. Never touch /output.
  * Run many probes (aim 40-80). Batch them in for-loops so it is cheap. Quote carefully.
  * Adversarially attack your own hypothesis: for every rule you state, try to find an input that breaks it.
  * The goal is a byte-exact Rust reimplementation using only std. Where behavior is byte-oriented rather than
    char-oriented (UTF-8 multibyte input), say so explicitly, because Rust's String indexing would panic there.


=== titleize ===
YOUR SLICE: titleize(word) — line 5. Also infer the humanize/underscore behavior it is built on.
Determine EXACTLY: how underscores, dashes, spaces, multiple/consecutive separators are turned into words; whether a
trailing "_id" (or "id") is stripped (probe 'user_id', 'post_id', '_id', 'id', 'userid', 'user_ids'); whether camelCase
input is split on case boundaries (probe 'myWord', 'MyWord', 'HTMLParser', 'aB', 'ABCdef'); which characters get
capitalized and whether the rest of each word is lowercased (probe 'hello WORLD', 'mcdonald', "o'brien", 'x-ray');
whether the acronym table is consulted; digits ('word2word', '2word'); empty string; leading/trailing separators;
non-ASCII bytes. State the pipeline (e.g. underscore -> humanize -> capitalize each word) precisely.

gotchas: The ONLY word separator is the space byte 0x20. Do NOT use char::is_whitespace or split_whitespace — tab, newline, CR, form feed, vertical tab, and NBSP do not split and do not reset the capitalize flag.
Do NOT use str::split(' ').map(capitalize).join(" ") — that is behaviorally equivalent here only by accident; safer and exactly right is the single in-place byte loop with a boolean flag.

Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Iterating `word.chars()` and using char::to_uppercase/to_lowercase is WRONG: it would turn 'É' into 'é' and 'ß' into 'SS'/'ss'. The binary leaves every byte >= 0x80 untouched. Iterate over bytes.

The capitalize flag is cleared even when toupper is a no-op. So a word beginning with '_', '-', a digit, a quote, or a UTF-8 lead byte gets NO capital letter anywhere: '_abc' stays '_abc', not '_Abc'.
Corollary: a word starting with a multibyte character is never capitalized ('éclair' -> 'éclair'), because the C3 lead byte absorbs the flag.

std::string indexing in C++ is infallible for i < size(); in Rust, `word[i..]`/`word.as_bytes()[i]` on a &str is fine but building a String from the mutated bytes must not assume validity if you extend this to arbitrary byte input. Remapping only ASCII a-z<->A-Z is UTF-8-safe, so from_utf8_unchecked is legitimate here; from_utf8().unwrap() is also fine for &str input but would panic on raw invalid-UTF-8 byte input.
Empty input must return empty output, not panic: the while loop condition `i < size()` guards it. Don't write code that touches index 0 unconditionally.
No locale is ever set (no setlocale call), so glibc runs in the "C" locale: toupper/tolower affect ONLY [a-z]/[A-Z]. Do not emulate any locale-specific mapping.

The asm sign-extends the byte (movsbl) before calling toupper/tolower, so 0x80..0xFF arrive as negative ints; glibc's tables are identity there. 0xFF (-1, i.e. EOF) also maps to itself. No UB-driven surprises observed.
Output byte length ALWAYS equals input byte length. Any implementation that trims, collapses runs of spaces, strips a trailing '_id', or inserts spaces at case boundaries is wrong.

Do not reuse a shared `capitalize()` helper if that helper is defined as 'uppercase first char, lowercase rest' over chars — line 6 (capitalize) and line 5 (titleize) may differ in their handling of high bytes; titleize needs the byte-level version.

Trailing '_id'/'id' stripping, case-boundary splitting, and the HTML/HTTP/XML/JSON/API acronym table all belong to humanize()/underscore()/camelize() and are NOT part of titleize. Do not wire them in.
The loop calls size() every iteration in C++ but never mutates length, so a plain Rust for-loop over iter_mut() is faithful.
unresolved: Whether the mutating in-place `operator[]` write could differ for a shared/COW string is moot: libstdc++ SSO strings are always uniquely owned after the copy, and a fresh copy is made at function entry, so the caller's argument is never mutated. Not separately probed by aliasing, since the CLI cannot express it.

humanize() and underscore() bodies were only surveyed via their callee lists (underscore: isupper/tolower/insert; humanize: regex + a std::map + toupper). Their exact semantics are outside this slice and, crucially, are NOT reachable from titleize, so they were not fully derived.
